#5483. Tech Moves: Microsoft loses a CVP to AWS and gains one from Alteryx; Lila Bio and BECU name execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 3, 2026 at 2:30 pm

— After more than 33 years at Microsoft, Mazhar Mohammed has left to become vice president of AWS Streaming and Messaging at Amazon.

Mohammed joined Microsoft as a software design engineer on Windows NT straight out of a master’s degree program. Over the decades, he also worked on messaging, mobile services and partner experience for cloud services. He most recently served as corporate VP for the commerce and fraud protection platform.

His LinkedIn post was short and to the point. Mohammed said he was “happy to share” the news, and the post featured a photo of an Amazon box with the message “Alexa, play ‘New Beginnings.’”

— Microsoft has named Chad Thompson as CVP of Agent Cloud, a group within the company developing technology that allows businesses to deploy AI agents and put them to work across their organizations.

“My view: enterprise is where AI pays off. Not in demos, but in measurable results. Lower costs, faster cycle times, better decisions, and work that gets done without someone pushing it along,” Thompson wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Thompson joins from Alteryx. He previously spent six years at Amazon, departing as general manager of Amazon Glow. Other past employers include Smartsheet, Exasol and Adobe.

— Gail Carpenter has been named as VP and chief financial officer of Global Entertainment and Advertising at Amazon. She was most recently CFO of Worldwide Stores Finance and has been with the company for 11 years.

— Seattle biotech startup Lila Bio has appointed Kimberly Ma as chief development officer. The company spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington and is using AI to design new proteins that can treat cancer with targeted radiation therapy. Last year it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop therapies for solid tumors.

Ma has 20 years of experience in oncology drug development, most recently as a leader at Abdera Therapeutics. She also worked at RayzeBio, where she led the clinical operations team and supported the company’s IPO and its $4.1 billion acquisition by Bristol Myers Squibb in 2024.

— The not-for-profit credit union BECU has named Geoffrey Fonga as VP of AI transformation. The member-owned organization is based in Tukwila, Wash.

“For years, I helped organizations adopt and scale AI as an advisor and a vendor,” Fonga said. “Now I get to do the harder, more rewarding part: leading that transformation from the inside.”

Fonga joins from DataRobot. He previously held leadership roles at McKinsey & Company and Wells Fargo.

— Andre Woodson Jr. has taken a new role at Amazon as manager of U.S. state and local policy communications and external affairs. Woodson was previously a regional field communications manager and has been with the company for more than 12 years.

— Hanna Grene has left Microsoft, where she served as global go-to-market and innovation leader for energy, to join Xcel Energy. She will lead the company’s newly established Enterprise Growth and Commercialization group, effective Nov. 16.

— Seattle-based RevealDx,which is developing AI technology for detecting potentially cancerous lung nodules, has made two leadership appointments:

— Enterprise software company LogicGate has named two new leaders to the business, which is headquartered in Chicago and has multiple C-suite executives based at its Bellevue, Wash., office. Steve Smith has joined as managing director of Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and Amanda Meglemre as general counsel.

— Former Cisco and Microsoft security executive Edna Conway was appointed to the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based tech company building accountability infrastructure for AI agents. Conway was with Cisco for 20 years before joining Microsoft in 2020 as VP and chief security and risk officer for Azure infrastructure.

— Avalanche Energy, a Seattle-based startup building fusion devices, has named Chris Riegel as head of talent acquisition. He joins from HiringKit, an HR company that Riegel co-founded. Former employers include Amazon and Unity Technologies.

In addition to chasing fusion, Avalanche is leading a team tackling DARPA’s nuclear battery challenge and launching FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies in Eastern Washington.

— Julie Averill, former chief information officer at lululemon and REI, has joined the UW Foundation Board, which helps raise philanthropic support for the university.

— Technology Alliance has appointed Jen Oleson, a senior director at Seattle-based consulting firm Slalom, to its board. Oleson will serve on the organization’s Research Capacity Committee.

— Ben Helsel has left Premera Blue Cross to join Kaiser Permanente, where he’ll serve as VP and general manager of commercial markets in Washington.

#5482. Coffee giant Dutch Bros made all of its executives, including the CEO, do a two-week bootcamp where they learned how to pour drinks and run stores

Dutch Bros CEO Christine Barone can do more than steer a $7.5 billion coffee chain—she can also hold her own behind the store counter. Like all other top leaders at the beverage giant, she embarked on a two-week bootcamp to learn the ropes of being a “broista.” And the chain’s workers weren’t afraid to call her out on mistakes.

“As I trained, people knew I was the CEO, and our teams would always point out when I was doing something wrong,” Barone tells Fortune. “That is one of the magical signs of a great culture that I need to make sure I build upon, because when my team cares so much about the customer that they’re going to tell the CEO that they were doing something wrong, I love that.”

The executive’s beverage training is part of the company’s “growth from within” model. Dutch Bros staffers, from store owners to senior managers, have been put through the course for years to understand the hard work of the chain’s 25,000 broistas churning out drinks. During the training, leaders complete six shifts of hands-on shop training, sharpening their hospitality skills, perfecting drink orders, and learning how to deliver on the values of speed, quality and service.

The chain says they witness first-hand how customer connections are made, and learn how to perfect drinks including the popular Golden Eagle coffee, so that everything tastes the same on Monday as it does on Wednesday. At the end, Dutch Bros leaders have to pass a “Flow” test, with questions ranging from drink recipes and company history to shop operations and culture. And the brand is serious about its standards; those who don’t pass have to retake the test.

Barone says the broista bootcamp reflects the vision of Dutch Bros’ founders: brothers Travis Boersma and the late Dane Boersma, who named the company in honor of their grandparents who immigrated from the Netherlands. Aside from gaining technical and hospitality expertise, she says the training nurtures “compelling futures” at the company, and lights a path for employees to work themselves up the chain of command.

“As we rolled it out to the more broader team across HQ, we were very thoughtful about making sure our marketing teams went through the training, especially the folks who are helping to design and make beverages,” the CEO explains. “Just thinking through: What are all those decisions we’re making that touch where the customer interaction is? And how do we ensure that everyone who is designing programs for our teams, or designing marketing programs, or designing new beverages, really understands what the shop environment feels like?”

After Starbucks and Dunkin’ Donuts, Dutch Bros is the third-largest coffee chain in the U.S. by sales and number of locations—and a huge hit among Gen Zers. But before ascending the caffeine mountaintop, the business was a humble roadside operation.

Their family dairy business was struggling, forcing the Boersma brothers to sell their cows and consider a new venture.

Their coffee business started off with a pushcart and 100 pounds of coffee beans back in 1992, with the brothers slinging espresso by the railroad tracks of Grants Pass, Oregon. Friends, relatives, and loyal customers kept their dream alive as the business grew. In 1994, their pushcart was upgraded to a drive-thru stand; and just two years later, they had expanded to six locations. The first Dutch Bros franchise opened for business in 2000.

The brand is known for its high-energy service and sugary drinks, which have since made their way to high school classrooms and office cubicles across the country. By 2018, it was already at 300 locations and employed 9,000 staffers, then private equity TSG Consumer Partners acquired a minority stake in Dutch Bros to grow it even more.

The years following were marked by major milestones, including going public, surpassing $1 billion in revenue, and beefing up its store count. Dutch Bros reported record-breaking revenue of $1.64 billion in 2025, up 27.9% year over year. And now, the brand boasts 37,000 systemwide employees and 1,273 Dutch Bros locations across 27 U.S. states. It hopes to grow its store footprint to 2,029 by 2029.

It can be difficult for businesses to preserve their home-grown culture as headcounts balloon, operations spread out, and outside investors get into the mix. One way to preserve it may be getting leaders to experience the business from the ground floor. The Dutch Bros CEO says that it has operators—a store or market leader responsible for running location operations—start off their career on the coffee line before moving up and into new markets. And as they advance into leadership and expand the number of locations they’re managing, they understand front-line issues and are skilled in building tight community connections.

“They’ll manage a region, so they’ll have their own set of shops that they’re managing. So why is that important?” Barone says. “Understanding this is the business that we’re in, and so when you have lived it yourself, your ability to understand where others on your team are starting from, you understand what that customer service feels like. That is important.”

Barone says that a “large number” of workers at HQ started off as broistas, enabling senior staffers to make decisions “through the right lenses.” That firsthand experience helps employees develop a sense of empathy that extends from the boardroom to the coffee counter—and serves them whether they stay at Dutch Bros, or choose to go elsewhere.

“When we’re great at hospitality, the definition for me is almost the ability to think through how someone else will experience something, more so than ourselves,” Barone says. “It really is great to be able to be empathetic…I think it’s a great skill if folks come up with us, or if they go and choose to do something else.”

Emma Burleigh is a reporter at Fortune, covering success, careers, entrepreneurship, and personal finance. Before joining the Success desk, she co-authored Fortune’s CHRO Daily newsletter, extensively covering the workplace and the future of jobs. Emma has also written for publications including the Observer and The China Project, publishing long-form stories on culture, entertainment, and geopolitics. She has a joint-master’s degree from New York University in Global Journalism and East Asian Studies.

#5480. Your Customers Are Using AI Search. They’re Still Googling You, Too. Here’s What Your Marketing Strategy Might Be Missing.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

A new audience-overlap finding is a useful corrective to the idea that AI search is replacing Google. And it changes how businesses should think about discovery and measurement.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I keep hearing a version of the same question from business leaders: Is AI search taking customers away from Google?

A new Similarweb audience-overlap figure offers a useful answer, with an important limit. In September, 93.7% of ChatGPT.com’s visitors also visited Google.com. The overlap ran the other way, too: 14.1% of Google.com’s visitors also visited ChatGPT.com, according to Search Engine Watch’s report.

That is not proof that someone asked ChatGPT about a product, then searched for it on Google. The data counts people who visited both websites during the month. It doesn’t show which one they used first, how often they searched, what they searched for or whether they bought anything. It also doesn’t capture the full use of either service through apps.

Those limits matter. But they don’t make the finding irrelevant. They tell us not to mistake channel overlap for channel substitution.

For years, marketers have organized discovery into tidy channels: search, social, referrals, paid media. AI assistants make that division harder to defend. A person might ask an AI tool to compare options, search a brand name in Google, watch a creator review, then visit a company’s site directly. The journey may cross several systems before the business gets a measurable click.

The Similarweb figure doesn’t prove that sequence. It does show why we shouldn’t assume that a visitor counted in an AI audience is a new person who has never used Google. Treating those groups as separate pools can lead to double-counting, inflated reach estimates and bad budget decisions.

I saw a version of this mistake when search was still new to many companies. Some treated SEO as a separate experiment instead of infrastructure for demand that already existed. The risk now is the reverse: treating AI discovery as a replacement for the search habits customers still have.

The better question isn’t which platform wins. It’s whether your brand is present, clear and credible when a customer moves between them.

The overlap stat also exposes a measurement problem. A customer might encounter a brand in an AI answer and later search for it by name. That later visit could show up as Google organic traffic, even if the earlier discovery helped create the demand. Or the AI interaction might never produce a visit at all. The audience-overlap data can’t tell us which happened.

That is why last-click reporting is a poor referee for this shift. A referral source can tell you where a session came from. It usually can’t tell you which earlier interactions made the brand worth looking up.

Google has begun giving site owners a clearer view of one part of the picture. Its Search Console generative AI performance report shows impressions for pages appearing in Google’s AI search features, including AI Overviews and AI Mode. That is useful visibility data, not proof of incremental traffic or revenue, and it doesn’t cover ChatGPT or other AI platforms.

Businesses should keep the measures separate. Track traditional search clicks, branded searches, qualified leads and sales. Alongside them, monitor which pages appear in Google’s AI features and whether your brand is cited in a consistent set of relevant AI prompts. Add a simple question to lead forms or post-purchase surveys: “Where did you first hear about us?” None of those signals proves, on its own, that AI caused a sale. Together, they can reveal patterns that last-click reports miss.

The response isn’t to split the marketing budget evenly between Google and AI. It’s to stop planning as if every platform reaches a different customer.

Keep investing in the parts of search that help customers find and evaluate you. Make sure the pages that explain your products, pricing and value are current. Understand which questions bring qualified prospects to your site. Then extend the same discipline to AI discovery: Check whether answer engines describe your business accurately, cite useful sources and include you when customers compare options.

Most importantly, connect the teams and dashboards. If SEO reports a decline in clicks while AI visibility rises, don’t declare one channel the winner and the other the loser. Look at branded search, lead quality, direct visits and conversion trends. Ask customers what influenced them. Compare the pattern over time, not just across one month’s traffic report.

I don’t read the 93.7% figure as evidence that Google is safe or that AI search is harmless to existing traffic. It doesn’t answer either question. I read it as a reason to be more precise: Customers can add a new way to discover a business without abandoning the old one.

Your customers may meet you in an AI answer and Google you before they act. The companies that understand both moments will make better decisions than the ones still asking which channel gets credit for the whole journey.

A new Similarweb audience-overlap figure offers a useful answer, with an important limit. In September, 93.7% of ChatGPT.com’s visitors also visited Google.com. The overlap ran the other way, too: 14.1% of Google.com’s visitors also visited ChatGPT.com, according to Search Engine Watch’s report.

That is not proof that someone asked ChatGPT about a product, then searched for it on Google. The data counts people who visited both websites during the month. It doesn’t show which one they used first, how often they searched, what they searched for or whether they bought anything. It also doesn’t capture the full use of either service through apps.

#5479. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

Disclosure: This is not trading or investment advice. Always do your research before buying any cryptocurrency or investing in any services. Follow us on X @nulltxnews.

Mark Arguinbaev is the founder of NullTX and owner of The Merkle, LLC, the publisher behind NullTX and The Merkle. Based in San Francisco, he sets editorial direction and standards for both sites and reviews the coverage published under his name. He is also the founder of Margin Systems.

#5478. Amazon rewrites its software engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 12:26 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 12:36 pm

Last month, a small team inside Amazon Web Services called Velocity Labs went from concept to the public release of a new open-source AI model in less than a week.

The group, whose existence hasn’t been previously reported, was formed in April. Velocity Labs has about 35 people, most of them in Seattle. The idea is to think beyond Amazon’s normal product-oriented approach, building quick prototypes in areas of AI that the company sees as underexplored and increasingly important to customers.

“We have noticed how the open-source community, and some of our competitors, experiment with new ideas, and deliver initial products fast,” the company says in job listings. “With Velocity Labs we are building an organization that can move faster, explore more, and make sure AWS is at the cutting edge of innovation in agentic AI.”

Inside the group, scientists and engineers work together, and they’re encouraged to cross over: engineers engage in research, and scientists do engineering work.

Velocity Labs is an example of the ways Amazon is trying “to create organizations that we think are going to be better suited to working with this new set of tools,” said Marc Brooker, an AWS vice president and distinguished engineer who leads the team.

For the vast majority of Amazon’s developers, he said, AI agents now write almost all the code that would have previously been written by hand.

Redefining the role: The team is part of Amazon’s larger rethinking of software development for the AI era, laid out in revised guidelines that the company’s engineering leaders sent to its developers earlier this year.

A letter that accompanied the guidelines, published last week under the byline of Michael “Terk” Terkowitz, a VP and distinguished engineer in Amazon’s stores business, advises engineers to learn AI now and to stay close to their customers and products.

The letter acknowledges that as Amazon has grown, some engineers and managers have become “less connected to their customers and business.”

Amazon has never published its underlying role guidelines for software engineers, and it declined to provide a copy of the revised version for this article. Brooker, one of the authors of the accompanying letter, said in an interview that the update emphasizes measuring engineers and teams by outcomes rather than inputs.

“We had seen these anti-patterns in the industry of folks really focusing on how many tokens are you spending, how many lines of code are you committing,” Brooker said, explaining that those kinds of measures don’t equate to customer value.

Asked whether AI use is part of performance reviews or promotions, Brooker said, “Not directly in a metrics sense.” It could factor in, he said, to the extent that it makes someone a stronger performer.

The letter doesn’t dismiss usage metrics entirely. Amazon has found that they “correlate well with the outputs that matter” and expects that to continue “for some time,” it says.

But what’s important, the letter says, is to use them “with care and judgement.”

Amazon engineers have described pressure to use AI tools. Three developers told The New York Times last year that managers were pushing them to use AI, raising output goals and becoming less forgiving about deadlines, with some coders saying their jobs had begun to resemble warehouse work. Amazon has set a goal for more than 80% of its developers to use AI each week, the Financial Times reported.

In May, Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard called KiroRank — which ranked employees by how much they used Kiro, the company’s AI coding tool — after finding that some were using the tool excessively just to climb the rankings, the FT reported.

Asked whether that episode was part of the impetus for the revised guidelines, Brooker said he didn’t recall the leaderboard or the details surrounding it.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing. Document why, share it with your community of peers, bring it to your manager, and work to find solutions.”

Letter accompanying the revised SDE role guidelines

How the work has changed: Two years ago, most Amazon developers were still writing their code by hand, Brooker said. Today, “for the vast majority of our developer population, almost all of their implementation code is agent generated rather than human written,” he said.

“That is a massive change in the way of working for software engineers,” he said.

Brooker said he used to spend much of his time in a traditional code editor or the command line, and now spends a lot more of it working with agent tools such as Kiro, Kiro Crew and Anthropic’s Claude Code, calling it “a complete change of tools.”

For the company, the transition hasn’t been seamless. In March, Amazon acknowledged that an engineer who followed inaccurate advice from an AI agent contributed to one of several outages on its retail site, though the company disputed a Financial Times report that junior and mid-level engineers would need senior engineers to sign off on AI-assisted changes.

Amazon also pushed back on an earlier FT report that a 13-hour disruption to an AWS service in December happened after engineers let its Kiro AI coding tool make changes, and the tool decided to “delete and recreate the environment.” Amazon blamed user error — a misconfigured role — and said it has since added safeguards, including mandatory peer review for production access.

Still, the letter acknowledges that today’s AI tools won’t help in every situation, and it says that’s OK as long as engineers can explain why.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the letter says. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.”

Inside Velocity Labs: The group is part of the agentic AI division led by Swami Sivasubramanian, which has organized much of its work around small teams of six to eight people, as GeekWire reported in June. Velocity Labs also includes the developers behind Strands, AWS’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

The model that Velocity Labs released last month, Strands Decider 2B, is designed to make quick, narrow decisions inside AI agents, such as which tool to use or where to route a request. It’s based on Qwen, an open model from Alibaba, and was released Oct. 1 along with the recipe used to train it.

Brooker built the original version on his own GPU at home after the startup TypeSafe AI unveiled Jev, a similar decision model, on Sept. 15, he wrote on his blog. “Every line of code was written by an agent,” he wrote, though he tried to make sure “the core ideas and insights were mine, or at least I understood them.”

Brooker described the team’s turnaround as less than a week from concept to public release. OpenAI announced a similar hosted service, its Decisions API, the same week, TechCrunch reported.

Brooker credited the team’s speed to its small size and a high level of trust: each person takes ownership of a piece of a project and asks for help when needed. He expects Amazon to create more teams like it, though not across the whole company.

Impact on jobs: Amazon has cut roughly 30,000 corporate jobs since late 2025. CEO Andy Jassy has said he expects AI to shrink the company’s corporate workforce over time.

At the same time, AWS CEO Matt Garman said in April that Amazon is “hiring just as many software developers as we ever had,” Business Insider reported. An Amazon spokesperson told the publication that more than 11,000 interns and early-career software engineers would join the company globally this year.

Asked whether AI will mean fewer engineers at Amazon, Brooker said, “I don’t think it changes the number of engineers.” The company wants engineers who take ownership, are curious and can learn quickly outside their areas of expertise, he said.

AI isn’t the right answer for every problem, Brooker said.

If the right tool is “an AI agent powered by a cutting-edge model, fantastic,” he said. However, he added, if it’s “three lines of Python code, that’s great too.”

#5477. How to Properly Lead a Team When the Founder Still Calls Every Shot

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Reporting to a founder is different from reporting to a manager. Here are four ways to make this special relationship work.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For more than a decade, founder-led companies have returned more than twice as much to shareholders as companies that are not founder-led, according to Bain. In tech, the multiple is higher still. The executives I speak with take roles at founder-led companies because they’re attracted to high returns. Then they discover the founder will not let go of the work the executive was hired to lead.

I coach C-suite executives who report to founders and co-founders, including COOs, CPOs, CTOs, chiefs of staff and heads of function. I also coach founders themselves, at companies ranging in size from a handful of employees to publicly traded behemoths. Most managing-up advice, my own included, assumes your boss holds a particular role, but this advice doesn’t stick when your founder is running a company they built themselves.

Every founder keeps a short list of tasks they will never hand over, no matter what the organizational chart says, and some of those tasks are likely on your job description.

I worked with a chief of staff who reported to a founder. In interviews and in their job description, they were told they would own strategy, operations and business development, but they quickly learned that they didn’t truly own them. Sure, they could have fought for the scope they were promised, but it would have been a losing battle. Instead, I coached them to focus on projects where they had real ownership.

Delegation can break down in the opposite direction, too. A COO I worked with ran board meetings but was never asked to manage board relationships or investor conversations. Her founder kept those tasks close to the vest. At the same time, he handed over responsibility for the entire budget to her and took little interest in even reviewing it. Through our coaching, she decided to loop him in more than he wanted and used the board meetings as a way to connect with board members and investors.

Ask your founder what they want to stay close to, then watch what happens over the next quarter. Ask again as the company scales, because the list will likely move. What a founder says they will hand over and what they actually hold onto are not always different.

Nearly every founder-led company has a small group of friends and peers whose input carries weight. They often look like co-founders, early employees, board members or an executive assistant who has been there since the start. In some cases, this group includes a family member with no formal ties to the company other than being related to the founder.

Over the years, I’ve coached clients to look far beyond the org chart when thinking about how to get things done. We spend sessions creating their own map of key individuals who influence the founder, both formally and informally.

In your first 90 days of a new job, it’s important to take special notice of whose wisdom your founder repeats and whose objection changes their mind. Build relationships with those people before you need them.

How a founder talks is often different from what they mean, and the translation depends on which type you are working with. I’ve seen two communication patterns come up repeatedly.

Visionary founders think out loud. They express a half-formed idea in a Monday meeting, but your team hears it as a mandate. They reprioritize their quarter unnecessarily around something the founder has already moved past, and your team ends up spending a weekend building a deck nobody asked for.

Conversely, operator founders speak in specifics. When they ask a passing question about a metric, your team should get to work and make sure they have the information they want. These founders mean what they say, and you need to listen.

In practice, this requires you to get clear on the type of founder you’re working with, as well as what they want from you and your team. You want to know whether an idea is just an idea that can stay half-formed or a real ask that requires action and follow-through. To find out, you need to ask directly.

Founder-led companies operate differently on purpose, which can make the signals of a toxic culture difficult to diagnose.

I coached a COO who never expected to work 40-hour weeks. She wanted something closer to 60. Her founder worked 80 to 100, without vacations or days off, and expected the same from his direct reports, because that is what he asked of himself. He expected her to care about the company as much as he did, without the equity that would have made that expectation reasonable.

I helped my client clarify whether this level of effort was due to a temporary build phase or his standard operating model. I also coached her to test whether she could keep up. It turned out that this was his standard operating model, which wasn’t anywhere near sustainable for her, so she ultimately left for a company that was a better match.

If you are trying to work out whether you are in a difficult stretch or part of a true mismatch, the following questions can help:

That last question tends to be the most helpful. If the answer is yes, you’re looking at a structural issue, and trying to adjust on your end won’t change it.

Reporting to a founder often asks more of you than reporting to a typical manager. Test what your founder will actually delegate, map the people they listen to, translate their words before you or your team acts on them and stay honest about whether the mismatch is a stretch or a structure. The executives who do this well build real scope within the space their founder leaves them. You’ve got this!

I also coach founders themselves, at companies ranging in size from a handful of employees to publicly traded behemoths. #5476. Filing: Amazon’s previously announced layoffs include 95 jobs in Washington state

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 6:11 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 7:26 am

A notice made public Tuesday evening, disclosing about 95 Amazon job cuts in Washington state, is part of the company’s previously reported layoffs in its retail business, not a new round of reductions, a spokesperson confirmed.

The filing lists software engineers, product managers and program managers among the affected employees. Most are based in Amazon’s Seattle offices, but others work in Bellevue and Redmond, at warehouses in Sumner and Pasco, or remotely.

Reuters reported in early October that Amazon was laying off fewer than 1,000 corporate employees, mainly in its Stores unit, which runs the company’s e-commerce business. Amazon confirmed to GeekWire at the time that “hundreds” of Stores employees were affected. The notice covers only employees based in Washington state.

“We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities,” Amazon said in a statement at the time.

Most affected employees were notified in October, including 43 on or about Oct. 7, when the Stores cuts were first reported. Others received notice in September or as early as July 3, according to the filing.

The federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act requires large employers to give workers and the government advance notice of mass layoffs. Washington’s version of the WARN Act generally requires 60 days’ notice when a covered employer eliminates 50 or more jobs within 30 days across its Washington operations, excluding part-time employees.

Amazon has made a series of smaller filings under the state law in the past year, including notices covering 121 jobs in August, 57 tech jobs earlier in the summer and 84 jobs last December.

The latest notice covers employees at 17 Amazon offices and warehouses in Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Sumner and Pasco, plus 15 remote workers in the state.

The list also includes risk managers, several directors and other senior employees. Employees who land other jobs inside Amazon before their separation dates won’t be laid off, the notice says.

The Stores cuts were much smaller than Amazon’s major corporate cutbacks since last fall. The company eliminated about 14,000 corporate roles globally in October 2025, including 2,303 in Washington, followed by another round in January that included 2,198 Washington employees.

#5475. Starfish Space loses contact with its Otter spacecraft, ending satellite inspection mission

by Alan Boyle on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:50 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 11:10 pm

Starfish Space says it can no longer receive data from its first full-scale Otter space vehicle, bringing a $15 million NASA mission to inspect inoperable satellites to a premature end.

In a LinkedIn post, the Tukwila, Wash.-based startup said its Otter 24C spacecraft was not able to complete all the objectives for the mission, known as Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY). “Starfish and NASA are exploring opportunities to fulfill mission objectives through other Starfish missions,” the company said.

The Otter spacecraft was sent into low Earth orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on Oct. 1. “Following a successful launch and deployment, Starfish established two-way contact with the spacecraft and successfully commanded Otter 24C, downlinking significant telemetry during early operations,” Starfish said.

However, the mission team lost contact with the oven-sized spacecraft during the commissioning process. “An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications,” the company said.

Starfish, NASA and Astro Digital determined that the spacecraft was unrecoverable.

In today’s update, Starfish said it is working closely with Astro Digital to fix the fault protection system and update testing procedures for future Otters.

“Developing new capabilities in space requires taking on difficult challenges, learning quickly and applying those lessons to what comes next,” Starfish said. “The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit.”

Greg Stover, director of the Advanced Research and Technology Division at NASA Headquarters, said in a news release that “commercial capabilities like Starfish’s are critical for a competitive U.S. space economy and strong American leadership in low Earth orbit.”

“Technology demonstrations allow us to quickly test new systems, learn from their performance, and iterate so that we are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with every mission,” Stover said. “NASA will continue taking on bold challenges in close collaboration with our industry partners.”

Several other Otter missions remain on tap — including a satellite disposal job for the Pentagon’s Space Development Agency, two commercial satellite servicing missions in geostationary Earth orbit, and two servicing missions for the U.S. Space Force.

Starfish Space is also continuing to test an Otter Pup prototype that was launched into orbit last year. Last week, it posted a video to LinkedIn showing a close approach to a target satellite known as ElaraSat. The company says it is preparing for a docking attempt “and a chance to make history.”

#5474. Rover hires Textio co-founder Jensen Harris and former Amazon exec Vik Rajagopal

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:07 am

Seattle-based pet care marketplace Rover is adding two executives to its leadership team: former Motus CFO Vik Rajagopal as chief financial officer and Textio co-founder Jensen Harris as president of marketplace, product and technology.

Rajagopal succeeds Charlie Wickers, who served as Rover’s CFO from 2022 to 2025. Harris succeeds Brent Turner, who was Rover’s president and chief operating officer before he was named CEO last year.

Rajagopal spent nearly a decade at Amazon, starting in 2011 as a finance lead for Amazon Global Selling, the program that helps sellers reach customers in other countries. He later became a general manager in Amazon’s retail business, running the U.S. shoes and luggage stores and the home store, as well as Amazon’s U.S. Vendor Success Program.

He left Amazon in late 2020 to become CFO of Logos, a maker of Bible study software backed by private equity firm Cove Hill Partners. He was promoted to CEO about a year later, replacing the company’s founder, and led Logos until April 2024. He was most recently CFO at Motus, which makes software that companies use to manage and reimburse employees who drive for work.

Earlier in his career, Rajagopal was an investment banker at Wells Fargo Securities and worked in corporate development at Symantec. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale and an MBA from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

“Rover is a Seattle company that was built the right way from day one — solving a real customer pain point with a strong product, solid economics, and a culture that is poised for long-term success,” Rajagopal said in a news release on Wednesday.

Harris co-founded Seattle-based Textio in 2014 with Kieran Snyder, his wife, after both worked on productivity software at Microsoft. The startup used AI to analyze workplace writing such as job posts and performance reviews. Harris was Textio’s CTO for nearly eight years, then chief experience officer, before taking over as CEO from Snyder in January 2024. He handed the CEO role to Colleen Gallagher in January 2026 and remains with Textio as founder emeritus.

Textio has raised $42.5 million from investors and went through rounds of layoffs in 2024 and 2025 under Harris. As CEO, he led the launch of Lavalier, an AI-based interview intelligence platform.

Before Textio, Harris spent more than 15 years at Microsoft, where he led the redesign of the Office user interface that produced the Ribbon, and later led user experience for Windows and the touch interface for the original Surface.

After leaving the CEO role at Textio, Harris founded Expedition 60, a firm that helps companies rework how they build software with AI.

“Our pets give us unconditional love, and they deserve the very best in return,” Harris said in a statement, adding that he shares a home with “three very opinionated cats.”

Rover was born at a 2011 Seattle Startup Weekend event, where venture capitalist Greg Gottesman pitched the idea. Aaron Easterly led the company as CEO for 14 years, taking it through the pandemic, a public offering and a $2.3 billion take-private deal with Blackstone in 2024. He stepped down last year and became executive chair, handing the CEO role to Turner.

Rover now operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe and Australia, and says sitters and walkers on its platform have provided 50 million bookings to date. Its brands include cat-sitting marketplaces Meowtel and Cat in a Flat, and Australia-based Mad Paws. Beyond sitting and walking, Rover now offers training in the U.S. and is testing other services.

#5473. Being ‘Good at Social Media’ Isn’t Enough to Run Your Business Accounts. Here’s What Is.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Invest in training your team, and your social media stops being a question mark and starts becoming one of your strongest business assets.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Small businesses do this every day. They hand off the Instagram social media account to a niece because she’s “always on her phone,” or have the youngest person in the office to run the social accounts by default. It’s understandable, and honestly, it’s a start! But managing social media for a business is a whole different ballgame. It takes real strategy, platform know-how, consistent execution and a clear understanding of what actually drives growth.

Here’s what I’ve learned working with clients across all kinds of industries: enthusiasm without training only gets you so far. Organic social media is one of the most powerful tools your business has, and it only delivers when the person running it knows what exactly they are doing. Here are seven reasons why training your social media team is one of the smartest moves you can make.

Paid ads are great, but organic social media is where your brand actually lives. It is how people discover you, decide if they trust you and choose to spend their money with you. Done well, it builds community, drives traffic and keeps you top of mind without a single dollar in ad spend. When I work with clients at Fix Your Search, one of the first things I do is help their team understand just how powerful this tool is, because most people underestimate it until they see a solid organic strategy in action.

That kind of impact does not happen by accident. It requires strategy, consistency and someone who understands how each platform works. Training is what gets you there.

This is the big one. Scrolling TikTok every night does not make someone qualified to manage your brand’s presence. Personal use and professional strategy are completely different skill sets. When I start training a client’s team, we talk about the difference between posting for fun and posting with purpose. Once that clicks, everything else starts to fall into place.

Here is the tricky part a lot of business owners do not talk about. If social media strategy is not in your forte, how do you teach it to someone else? You cannot spot mistakes you cannot see. When a client brings me in, the business owner does not have to be the expert. I take their team members from the very beginning, walking them through what good social media management actually looks like, step by step, so there is no guesswork on anyone’s end.

What works on Instagram is not what works on LinkedIn. What thrives on TikTok might flop on Facebook. Each platform has its own audience behavior, content format and algorithm logic, and not knowing the difference is one of the fastest ways to waste your team’s time and energy.

Platform-specific training is a core part of how I work with my clients. We always start with the fundamentals: understanding each platform’s purpose, writing captions that earn engagement, building a content calendar that makes sense and reading analytics without the eyes glazing over. That foundation is everything.

The algorithm loves relevance. Trending formats, sounds and topics get shown to more people, plain and simple. But jumping on a trend blindly without understanding how to make it work for your brand can hurt more than help. That is why trend awareness is a dedicated part of the training I do with my clients. When a team knows how to work with trends, reach can grow fast and it is always exciting to watch it happen.

Training is not one single afternoon session. Social media platforms change constantly, and a strategy that worked six months ago might be hurting your reach today. When I train a client’s team, I stay involved over time. We review what is working, adjust to algorithm updates and keep building on what the team learns. Everything I do is tailored to the specific business, because what makes sense for a local bakery looks completely different from what makes sense for a nightclub or an upscale restaurant.

Your social media accounts are often the very first impression a potential customer has of your business. That’s why, when I train a client’s team, I always tie the work back to this bigger picture. We’re not just filling a content calendar. We are crafting a presence that earns trust, attracts the right people and reflects the business at its best.

When proper training is in place, the results speak for themselves. Engagement climbs, reach grows and the team member who once second-guessed every post starts owning their role with real confidence. Watching that shift happen is honestly the most rewarding part of the work I do.

If your social media is not delivering the results you hoped for, the answer is almost never to scrap everything and start fresh. More often than not, the missing piece is proper training. Organic social media is a long game, and every business that plays it well has one thing in common: a team that genuinely knows what they are doing, why they are doing it and how to keep getting better. That kind of expertise does not appear overnight, but it is absolutely buildable. Invest in training your team the right way, and your social media stops being a question mark and starts becoming one of your strongest business assets.

#5472. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

#5471. Finpilot raises $10M for AI agents that handle the grunt work for institutional investors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:04 am

Seattle startup Finpilot, which uses AI agents to take the paperwork off the plates of people who invest money for hospitals, pension funds and foundations, has raised $10 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Bay Area venture firm Lobby Capital, with participation from Madrona, which led Finpilot’s $4 million seed round in 2024. Finpilot, which has raised about $14.5 million since its 2023 founding, plans to use the new funding to expand its product and hire across the company.

Its customers include in-house investment teams at institutions and firms that manage money on their behalf. In the industry, they’re known as allocators, because they spread capital across outside fund managers. Much of their information arrives from fund managers as PDFs and spreadsheets, and someone has to read the reports, pull out the numbers and enter them into the right systems.

Finpilot pulls that information into one place and has its agents handle much of the work. The idea is to let investment teams spend their time on judgment and decisions, not on reading data from documents and typing it into a database, said Lakshay Chauhan, Finpilot’s co-founder and CEO, in an interview.

“Nobody wakes up like, ‘All right, I’m excited to do that,'” he said.

It’s a change of course for the company. When GeekWire covered its seed round, Finpilot was building a ChatGPT-style tool for analysts researching public companies. It shifted to allocators in mid-2024, Chauhan said, after concluding that AI added only marginal value in public markets, where Bloomberg and S&P Capital IQ had already organized most of the data.

“There’s no Bloomberg for what they do,” he said of allocators.

Customers include Seattle Children’s, Children’s Health in Dallas, Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming, the Wyoming Retirement System, outsourced investment firm TIFF, and Seattle wealth management firm Laird Norton Wetherby. Some of those institutions hadn’t changed their core systems in 15 years, Chauhan said.

Finpilot has about 28 institutional customers in all, and revenue has grown tenfold since the start of the year, he said. It hasn’t lost a customer yet, he noted.

How it works: Finpilot pulls an institution’s data from its portfolio management system, document storage and other sources into a single record, matching each fund, holding and client to one identifier. Users ask questions in a chat window and set up agents to handle recurring work.

In an example Chauhan described, an agent could review updates from 35 private equity managers at the end of a quarter, figure out what changed and point an analyst to the three things that need attention. Agents also prepare briefings before meetings with fund managers, and they ask a person for approval when a step needs one.

Some customers run Finpilot alongside their existing software. Others have used it to replace older customer relationship management and research management systems, where investment teams log their dealings with fund managers.

Chauhan said Finpilot most often gets compared with general-purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, including finance-focused versions like Claude for Financial Services, and with legacy CRM vendors.

Chauhan said the difference is accuracy. A 10-page report from a chatbot has to be checked number by number before it goes to a chief investment officer. In Finpilot, every number links back to the document it came from, so it can be checked.

In finance, he said, “you cannot be wrong.”

Finpilot runs its own in-house model for the high-volume job of reading financial documents, and uses models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for other tasks. It doesn’t train AI models on customer data and keeps each customer’s data separate, Chauhan said.

Founders: Chauhan grew up in India and came to the U.S. for a master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He interned at Boeing in Seattle, but when he graduated, he said, many full-time aerospace jobs required U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, and he was in the country on a visa.

He went to work for an engineering optimization software company and studied quantitative investing on the side. That led him to a paper by John Alberg, co-founder of Seattle investment firm Euclidean Technologies, which uses machine learning to pick stocks. Chauhan called Alberg repeatedly to propose working together, and Alberg eventually hired him. Chauhan later led AI at Euclidean.

Alberg is Finpilot’s co-founder and executive chairman but isn’t involved in day-to-day operations. His late father, Tom Alberg, co-founded Madrona.

Finpilot has about 14 employees, up from four in 2024. All are based in Seattle except one in Boise, Idaho. The company recently moved into the AGC Building on Lake Union after outgrowing its old office.

What’s next: Finpilot plans to fill six or seven jobs in the next few months, in product, marketing, client success, sales and business development, and about as many early next year.

Part of the money will go to implementation teams, Chauhan said. Their job is to sit down with each customer, learn how its investment team works and show it how to redo that work with AI agents.

#5469. Greenwashing Won’t Save You — How Gen Z Is Rewriting the Rules of Brand Authenticity

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Discover how Gen Z is redefining brand authenticity, challenging greenwashing and demanding transparency, sustainability and real action.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Walk into any corner store or scroll past a sponsored post, and you see it right away. Everything is suddenly “eco-friendly,” “sustainably sourced” or “carbon-neutral.” Companies slap a leaf icon on a plastic wrapper, paint the box olive green and call it a day.

They think this trick still works. It doesn’t.

If your marketing plan leans on empty claims to win over younger buyers, you’re playing a risky game. Greenwashing won’t save your startup. It might actually sink it faster than bad cash flow. Gen Z is rewriting the rules of brand honesty, and they have zero patience for corporate spin.

For two decades, big brands got away with soft marketing. Slap a vague promise about 2050 goals on a billboard, hire a PR agency to write a press release about planting trees and watch sales climb.

Gen Z grew up with a phone in their hand and a search bar at their fingertips. They don’t read your ad copy and take it at face value. They check your supply chain. They search your brand name on TikTok to see if employees are calling out bad workplace habits. They can even look up your parent company’s tax filings.

When a brand gets caught lying about its footprint, the backlash is fast, loud and it doesn’t go away. A fake green label doesn’t make you look responsible. It makes you look dishonest.

Young shoppers don’t expect your startup to be perfect. They know running a business takes resources and that shipping physical goods creates carbon output. What actually bothers them is the theater.

Take a small digital-first startup that sells modular workspace gear. Instead of hiding behind vague terms like “100% Earth-Friendly,” they list the exact components: 80% recycled aluminum, 20% new ABS plastic because of structural limits, made in a factory that runs on a grid with a high coal mix.

That kind of honesty instantly sets them apart from competitors shouting about saving the planet.

Gen Z wants hard facts over soft poetry. They’d rather buy from a business that admits where it falls short than one that pretends to have no flaws at all.

To win customer trust today, startups need to rethink how they talk to people. Here’s how honest brands are changing the story:

Show the receipts: Don’t just say your sourcing is ethical. Prove it. If you run a fast-casual food stall, put the actual invoices from local farm suppliers near your register or post them online every week.

Name the trade-offs: If recycled paper packaging doubles your unit cost and pushes up your retail price, just say so. Customers respect the honesty.

Stop waiting to be perfect: You don’t need a flawless environmental record to speak up. Share your current numbers today, set short-term goals for next month and report back when you fall short.

Modern shoppers know every purchase involves some kind of trade-off. When you pretend your product has zero impact, you insult their intelligence.

Take a modern specialty tea brand as an example. Instead of claiming their tea bags are fully biodegradable, when most actually need industrial composting facilities that regular city systems don’t have, they put a warning label right on the front of the pouch:

“These tea bags need commercial high-heat composting. If you toss them in your garden, they’ll take years to break down. Here’s how to dispose of them the right way.”

That one blunt line builds more brand trust than a million-dollar ad campaign built on fluffy green claims. It shows respect for the buyer’s intelligence.

If you want your business to survive this shift, you need to drop the corporate buzzwords and rebuild how you talk to people, starting now.

Cut words like “green,” “pure,” “natural” and “conscious” from your site unless you back them up with a specific third-party certification or a real number. If a claim can’t be checked, delete it.

Use your social channels to show operational hiccups. If a supplier fails to meet your material standards, post about the delay. Explain why you turned down the shipment. Turn your operational struggles into proof of your standards.

Big-budget, super-polished video ads read as dishonest to an audience raised on user-generated content. A quick, unedited founder video shot on a phone explaining a packaging decision lands far deeper than a slick commercial.

Gen Z isn’t asking every business to solve global problems on its own. They’re asking businesses to stop using those problems as a sales tactic.

If your product is good, let it stand on its own. If your operations are still a work in progress, show the process. Drop the green paint, publish your real numbers and talk to your customers like actual people.

Trust is not something you buy with a clever campaign anymore. It’s something you earn by showing up, dropping the spin and telling the whole truth every single time.

Walk into any corner store or scroll past a sponsored post, and you see it right away. Everything is suddenly “eco-friendly,” “sustainably sourced” or “carbon-neutral.” Companies slap a leaf icon on a plastic wrapper, paint the box olive green and call it a day.

They think this trick still works. It doesn’t.

#5468. Amazon plans its first large-scale data centers in Washington state as residents raise concerns

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:36 am

Amazon is moving toward building its first large-scale data centers in Washington state, with a proposed campus in Walla Walla County and a second in the Tri-Cities that the company confirmed this week.

The expansion into Amazon’s home state comes amid nationwide pushback against the rapid deployment of new AI data centers. Tuesday’s election underscored the scrutiny facing data center developers, with voters in communities across several states backing limits on new projects. In Eastern Washington, the Amazon proposals have drawn calls for greater environmental oversight and a temporary halt to data center development.

Amazon already has a substantial footprint in neighboring Oregon, where industry tracker Baxtel lists 64 AWS data center sites. Expansion there has divided communities, with residents pushing for restrictions over power and water concerns while some Eastern Oregon officials warn that slowing development would jeopardize jobs and tax revenue.

Both proposed Washington campuses would initially include three data center buildings. The Walla Walla County site covers roughly 134 acres in Wallula Gap, while the Tri-Cities campus is on a 1,000 acre property in the city of West Richland and could eventually grow to 21 buildings. The company is already operating smaller data centers in the state, including Seattle.

The Tri-City Herald first reported Monday that Amazon was behind the West Richland project. The company plans to hold a community open house Nov. 19 to discuss the proposal.

A full build-out of the West Richland campus could create more than 1,000 full-time data center jobs, Amazon said. Dallas real estate firm Trammell Crow initially purchased the property from the estate of agricultural businessman Frank Tiegs, who died in 2024, before selling it to Amazon.

Nearby residents have raised concerns about the planned campus, in part because of its proximity to about 200 homes. Residents asked the local city council to approve a temporary moratorium, but at a meeting Tuesday evening, council members adopted rules that removed a data center noise exemption, banned them in light industrial zones, and prohibited cryptocurrency mining. The council failed to pass a moratorium, NonStop Local reported.

Amazon says the upcoming open house will give residents an opportunity to ask questions about the planned development. A spokesperson described a “science fair” format, with booths hosted by experts discussing water and energy usage, job creation, noise and environmental impacts.

“We’re committed to growing responsibly and we want the community to leave the Open House with a better understanding of this project and what it could mean for the area,” the spokesperson said via email.

At Wallula Gap, a recent public-comment period offers an indication of the scrutiny Amazon faces.

Of the 706 submissions received during a 30-day comment period that closed Oct. 12, only 23 — about 3% — supported the project, according to an analysis by the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin. Most of the supportive comments came from the area, and many predicated their support on more stringent oversight of the proposed facility near the Columbia River.

More than 500 submissions came from outside Walla Walla County, according to the Union-Bulletin. Many included template language calling for an Environmental Impact Statement — a higher level of environmental assessment than currently required for the campus.

The proposed facility is located at the Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. The three proposed single-story data center buildings would create approximately 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

The land is zoned for “industrial agriculture – mixed” applications, which the company said includes data centers. Amazon’s involvement in the project was first reported by the Tri-City Herald in February.

Amazon’s FAQs for the two sites address several issues raised by residents, including electricity costs and water use.

Rising electric bills nationwide and the climate impacts of new gas power plants and backup diesel generators have made energy use a top concern. Amazon said it will work with local utilities and other officials “to ensure that our data centers do not raise electricity bills for people in our communities.”

The company reports that it matched all electricity consumed across its global operations with renewable energy sources in 2023 and 2024. That annual, company-wide accounting measure does not mean each facility runs on renewable electricity around the clock.

Amazon also points to its investment of “billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects,” including a proposed small modular reactor plant near the Tri-Cities that could come online in the 2030s.

“This project will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said in its FAQ.

Amid concerns about water shortages, Amazon touts water-use rates that it says beat other tech companies and are much lower than irrigated farming. Those rates, however, do not include water used in electricity generation. Many power plants use water to produce steam that drives electricity-generating turbines and for cooling, with some water lost through evaporation.

At both locations, Amazon says it will pay 100% of its property taxes rather than seek tax breaks for building in the communities. The company says its taxes are higher than most industrial uses and directly support schools, roads, fire and police, and other services.

Beyond addressing concerns about its data centers, Amazon is making a broader case for why communities should welcome them. Last month, the company launched its Built Together initiative, committing more than $1 billion in additional investments over five years to U.S. communities where it operates data centers. The funding supports efforts including free community college, energy upgrades for homes and buildings, and workforce training.

In announcing the program, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman framed data center development as part of a global race for AI dominance. He warned that local and state moratoriums could harm the U.S. economy and national security.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman said. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

In West Richland, residents will have an opportunity to question Amazon’s plans — and the assurances accompanying them — at the company’s upcoming open house.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/5 to note that Amazon is operating smaller-scale data centers in Washington, but not campuses of the scope being proposed in Eastern Washington.
