#5426. October 29, 2019

Chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in New Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

More specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he says that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a new sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”

Park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own company. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a new home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

The now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the company has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as quickly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

#5425. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw $398.62 million in net daily outflows, led by Fidelity’s FBTC ($164 million), while 44,857 ETH left spot Ethereum ETFs.

Binance posted a record $15.4 billion weekly net outflow following a $6.3 billion hack the FBI attributed to North Korea.

This week’s key US triggers are the midterm elections and JOLTS (Tuesday), ISM services (Wednesday), the Fed balance sheet (Thursday) and Nonfarm Payrolls (Friday).

The crypto market greeted Tuesday morning, November 3, with a massive wave of margin position closures. Over the past 24 hours, the positions of 94,997 traders were forcibly liquidated for a total of $386.42 million, with 88% of all losses ($339.92 million) falling on long contracts, while Bitcoin ($100.74 million) and Ethereum ($49.31 million) led in liquidation volume as per CoinGlass.

A strong bearish skew persists in the US spot ETF sector: the net daily outflow from BTC funds amounted to $398.62 million, with the main blow falling on the Fidelity fund (FBTC), which saw $164 million leave. The current daily outflow has spread across the entire line of exchange-traded products: SOL funds lost 129.19 thousand coins, outflows from XRP products amounted to 128.54 thousand tokens, and the specialized HYPE and ZEC funds shed 85.07 thousand and 13.53 thousand coins, respectively. Major operators are preemptively pulling liquidity out of volatile instruments ahead of the US midterm elections.

Amid the decline in market capitalization, a sharp split among participants has emerged: while retail investors are locking in losses en masse and most whales are betting on a decline, some large on-chain operators are opening aggressive counter-trend positions on decentralized exchanges.

The main event of the morning session was the actions of an unknown major player on the Hyperliquid platform, who, despite the overall market decline (NEAR dropped to $3.79, BNB to $697.67), stubbornly holds an XRP long worth tens of millions of dollars, turning the contract into the main barometer of local altcoin resilience.

The decentralized futures platform Hyperliquid is currently accumulating peak institutional volumes. At the same time, on-chain analytics of top wallets with balances of $1 million or more shows a strong bearish skew in open interest.

Of these wallets' total open positions of $4.5 billion, short contracts (shorts) account for $3.08 billion. Their long volume is limited to a modest $1.46 billion.

Leviathan addresses with positions of $50 million or more are almost unanimously betting on a further market decline. Against this grim backdrop, the long position of wallet '0x31b1ecf848443472e34d204a134812d86ab01434' remains the largest and riskiest counter-trend position in the system.

The whale holds 35.03 million XRP tokens. The notional value of the open position is $44.05 million at 10x Cross leverage.

The average entry price is $1.1298. At the peak of the morning momentum, the whale's unrealized profit exceeded $4.47 million, which amounts to more than 101% net return on the margin capital invested.

At the same time, the account's overall result is far from ideal: due to overall asset volatility, this wallet's net PnL over the past 30 days has fallen by $8.45 million.

The critical threshold in this whole story remains the forced liquidation price. The automatic position closure threshold sits at $0.9626.

The current XRP market price of around $1.2558 leaves the trader a buffer of about 23% to the liquidation point.

Large wallets' XRP positions on Hyperliquid are also skewed toward the bears. Against long positions of $55.70 million stands a massive wall of shorts worth $80.93 million. Nearly 80% of these longs belong to a single whale.

This morning's news backdrop points to a massive and painful restructuring of the entire market infrastructure. The central theme remains a severe liquidity crisis on centralized exchanges.

$6.3 billion Binance hack and the FBI's position: The agency officially attributed the attack to North Korean state cyber units. An analysis by lawyers at Reed Smith and Lathrop GPM showed that the exchange's insurance policies will not cover the damage. Standard D&O insurance protects only top management, while war exclusion clauses fully rule out payouts in the event of cyberwarfare waged by foreign states.

Record outflow of $15.4 billion: The weekly net capital outflow from Binance hit an all-time high. This volume exceeds the individual reserves of Bybit or Bitfinex and surpasses the combined balance of Gate, Bitget and KuCoin, which keeps the price of BNB at local lows.

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao's loud statements about rising risks to the financial system from automated AI-powered cyberattacks came amid the incident at the exchange he created, which showed the ineffectiveness of classic defense mechanisms against coordinated cyber operations. Zhao stressed that commercial banks, due to outdated IT architecture, are more vulnerable than crypto platforms.

Against this backdrop, decentralized protocols are confidently expanding their institutional presence. Hyperliquid's annual revenue has reached $713 million, and trading volume in perpetuals on stocks and commodities via HIP-3 has exceeded $500 billion. Building on these technologies, the operator of the New York Stock Exchange (ICE) and Kraken are already preparing to launch regulated futures in the US with White House support.

Meanwhile, serious changes are also taking place at the level of the largest L1 ecosystems. House of Stake (NEAR Protocol) participants approved the deflationary initiative HSP-029 with 99.96% of the vote, reducing annual emissions from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. Daily issuance of new tokens is being cut from 89,500 to 57,300, while amid the general market decline the asset briefly dropped to $3.79.

Skepticism is meanwhile growing in the Ripple camp: the company reports that issuance of its dollar token RLUSD has surpassed $1 billion through partnerships with trust banks, but XRP holders are voicing open dissatisfaction. RLUSD is a centralized asset subject to freezing under US law, while XRP's decentralized status is not yet reflected in its market valuation.

At the same time, the Ethereum Foundation launched a platform for using the network as digital public infrastructure (DPI) for governments. Case studies on digital identity in Bhutan and confidential humanitarian aid systems have been published. At Devcon 8 in Mumbai, Vitalik Buterin called for developing verifiable code to minimize dependence on closed software and AI systems.

In the coming sessions, capital flows in the crypto market will be largely determined by external macroeconomic and political triggers. Investors and market makers need to keep the following critical factors in focus:

US Congressional midterm elections: The main political factor of this Tuesday, forcing large funds to preemptively close margin positions, cut leverage and hedge risks ahead of a change in the regulatory landscape.

Official JOLTS labor market report: Tuesday's release of job openings data will determine the short-term dynamics of the US dollar index and directly affect liquidity in high-risk assets.

ISM non-manufacturing business activity indices: Wednesday's statistics will highlight the real state of the US economy and shape the medium-term sentiment of major futures market operators.

Fed balance sheet on Thursday and Friday's Nonfarm Payrolls report: The key macroeconomic triggers of the week, which will lock in the final direction of capital flows through the end of the month.

#5422. JPMorgan and Mastercard back Seattle startup Firmly’s bet on AI shopping agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 7, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 7, 2026 at 10:30 am

Firmly, a Seattle-area startup that helps online retailers sell through AI shopping assistants, raised a $15 million Series A round led by Squarepoint Capital, with participation from J.P. Morgan Payments, Mastercard, Samsung Next and others.

The company, founded in 2019, connects retailers’ existing online stores to AI assistants, marketplaces and other shopping channels, so people can buy products inside those third-party apps and services without going to retailers’ websites. Retailers keep their own payment providers and customer relationships.

“Every new AI assistant, marketplace or shopping platform is another place to sell. But connecting to each one can take serious engineering, because catalogs, inventory, payments, and checkout all have to work together,” wrote Kumar Senthil, Firmly’s co-founder and CEO, in a blog post announcing the round.

Mastercard is a commercial partner as well as an investor. Firmly handles the merchant side of Mastercard Agent Connect, a service launched in September to link merchants, AI agents and payment providers through a single integration.

Senthil told Axios Pro that Mastercard is recruiting merchants for the service, giving Firmly a route to new customers.

Firmly charges merchants $2,000 to $15,000 a month, depending on the total value of merchandise they sell, Senthil told Axios. He said connecting a merchant took four to six weeks in 2024 and now takes a day or less, including testing.

The company lists Best Buy, Furniture.com and Backcountry among its retail customers. RetailMeNot and an AI shopping app called Wizard also use its technology.

The funding comes as AI shopping agents move into the mainstream. Meta’s Muse assistant can browse retail sites and buy items with a user’s approval. Amazon has blocked Muse from its site and is suing Perplexity over a shopping agent in the startup’s Comet browser.

Firmly takes a different approach from those agents. Instead of having software click through a retailer’s web pages, it connects directly to the retailer’s systems with its permission.

Firmly also launched Ask Agent, an AI shopping assistant for retailers’ own websites. Shoppers describe what they want, get product recommendations and can check out without leaving the chat.

Other investors in the round include Alumni Ventures, ARK Invest, Benhamou Global Ventures, Granada Funds, Hike Ventures, The Mercantile Companies and Versus Ventures.

The round brings Firmly’s total funding to about $20 million. The company had raised $5.2 million when it partnered with Perplexity in March 2025 on shopping features inside the AI search app.

Senthil spent eight years at Microsoft and later led e-commerce products at Samsung. He co-founded Firmly with Damien Balsan, a co-founder of LoopPay, the mobile payments startup acquired by Samsung, and Murali Krishnamurthy, Firmly’s CTO and a former chief technical architect for Samsung’s U.S. and global e-commerce business.

#5421. October 31, 2019

Album VC, a Lehi, Utah-based early-stage venture firm that’s been known until now as Peak Ventures, just gathered up $75 million in capital commitments for its third early-stage fund.

The development shows investor confidence in Album’s young team, which came together in 2014 after the founder of Zinch — a site connecting colleges and students that sold to the ed-tech company Chegg in 2011 — decided to try his hand at investing in other startups.

As that founder, Sid Krommenhoek — who stayed on with Chegg for several years, running its international efforts — explains it, “I thought I’d do another startup. But I also knew from our own experience in struggling to raise money the need for more capital in Utah, and I thought having that operator-entrepreneur perspective could be useful.”

A first fund, like many in the industry, was more of an experiment, though it was a decent $23 million, thanks largely to the support of Chegg CEO Dan Rosensweig, who was early to commit capital to the fund. A second ($56 million) fund followed when Krommenhoek and John Mayfield — a friend who joined him from a marketing role at Qualtrics — began investing more seriously in their backyard and beyond.

They were soon joined by a third investor, Diogo Myrrha, who began as a principal with the firm and is now a general partner. Explains Krommenhoek of one of the many things that binds the three Brigham Young University grads, “We all came into Utah’s orbit when it wasn’t necessarily a place where you could live out your career, but that’s changed.”

#5420. Bitcoin ETF Attracts $75M as Goldman Sachs Calls December Fed Rate Cut

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin ETF demand returned on November 4 as Bitcoin recovered above $81,000, but Wall Street’s outlook for Federal Reserve rate cuts remains uncertain. Goldman Sachs pushed its expected Fed rate cuts back by one quarter, citing persistent inflation and a labor market that remains resilient. The bank now expects reductions in December 2026 and March 2027.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF recorded $74.6 million in net inflows, ending three consecutive sessions of withdrawals totaling $1.16 billion. Fidelity’s FBTC led the recovery, while BlackRock’s IBIT continued losing capital.

Fidelity’s Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund attracted approximately $236.7 million on November 4. Bitwise’s BITB added $15.2 million, while ARK Invest’s ARKB received $19.9 million.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust moved in the opposite direction, recording $201.2 million in outflows. The withdrawals extended IBIT’s four-session losing streak to $935 million. These mixed flows show that institutional demand has not returned uniformly across the market.

Bitcoin also recovered from a seven-week low near $75,600 during the November 3 election period, climbing back above $81,000 today. The rebound followed market stabilization after the U.S. midterm elections, although analysts cautioned against attributing the recovery to a single catalyst.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Goldman Sachs now expects the Federal Reserve to deliver its next two rate cuts in December 2026 and March 2027, pushing both reductions back by one quarter.

The revised forecast shows concerns that energy costs could keep core personal consumption expenditures inflation near 3% throughout the year. Goldman economist David Mericle said lower inflation readings and further labor market softening would likely be necessary for the Fed to cut rates before year-end.

The bank maintained its projected terminal rate range of 3% to 3.25%, while acknowledging that the Fed could decide against additional cuts if economic conditions remain strong.

Bank of America adopted an even more cautious outlook, removing its expected 2026 rate cuts and moving them into the third quarter of 2027. This shift creates a more challenging macro backdrop for Bitcoin, which often benefits when borrowing costs fall and liquidity conditions improve.

But the latest Bitcoin ETF inflows suggest some investors are still willing to increase exposure despite the delayed easing outlook. The contrast between returning fund demand and a more cautious Fed forecast gives Bitcoin traders two competing signals.

Institutional buying could help support prices if inflows continue, while elevated interest rates may limit the liquidity available for risk assets.

Something potentially enormous could be approaching for Tesla (TSLA) by January 1, 2027. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts that TSLA stock could be a standout performer through Q4 and into 2027, based on a hypothetical landmark catalyst that isn’t impossible.

The concept focuses on Tesla obtaining widespread regulatory approval for unsupervised full self-driving robotaxi operations in several major markets, while also scaling up the production and deployment of Optimus humanoid robots beyond current expectations.

In this scenario, Tesla would quickly shift from primarily an electric vehicle manufacturer to a high-margin platform company centered on autonomy and robotics. This transformation could open up multi-trillion-dollar markets and significantly increase the company’s stock valuation.

On the higher timeframes, TSLA has been consolidating in the $390–$415 region after a recovery from lower levels earlier in the year. Price continues to hold above key intermediate supports while facing resistance around the $420–$450 zone.

In a standard bull market for growth and technology stocks, a sustained breakout above $480–$520 would confirm intermediate strength and open the path to higher-cycle targets.

Under the extreme robotaxi approval and Optimus scaling scenario outlined above, clearing significant resistance levels would likely trigger powerful measured-move extensions and multi-cycle projections from the longer-term base.

Momentum indicators currently sit in neutral-to-constructive territory with substantial room to run into the strong overbought readings typical of high-beta technology rallies.

Key nearer-term supports sit near $380–$390 and $350–$360; holding those levels would keep the broader recovery structure intact.

More importantly, Tesla confirmed that production of Optimus humanoid robots has begun on high-volume lines in Fremont, marking a shift from prototypes to early manufacturing.

On the autonomy side, the Cybercab robotaxi service continues to expand, with the Austin fleet growing rapidly, plans to launch in Dallas, and an ambition to deliver the first Cybercabs to customers by the end of 2026.

Unsupervised robotaxi miles have increased sharply, while Full Self-Driving subscriptions remain on a strong upward trajectory. Tesla has also entered volume production of the Semi.

While near-term profits remain under pressure from heavy investment, these operational milestones reinforce the narrative of Tesla evolving beyond vehicles into high-margin autonomy and robotics platforms.

Under this highly speculative scenario, and assuming supportive market conditions return, Tesla (TSLA) could reach between $1,800 and $3,000, with a stretch target toward $4,500+ by January 1, 2027.

This remains pure speculation and entertainment, not a realistic base-case outlook. The catalyst would require extraordinary regulatory progress and execution on robotaxi and Optimus at a scale that is currently highly unlikely.

#5414. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5413. Hyperliquid (HYPE) Rallies as CFTC Approves First-Ever US Stock Perpetuals

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Hyperliquid’s native token (HYPE) responded with confident growth to the historic decision of the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), which for the first time allowed trading of perpetual futures on individual stocks (Equity Perpetuals).

The regulatory shift de facto legitimizes a product that developed predominantly in DeFi ecosystems and opens the way for the institutional expansion of Hyperliquid’s infrastructure, which served as the trigger for the asset’s rally.

According to the CFTC release of November 3, 2026, equity perpetual contracts received the status of security futures under joint CFTC and SEC oversight, with the possibility of trading on dual-registered exchanges.

Today, equity perps can begin trading for the first time on @CFTC registered exchanges. This move reflects my commitment to ensuring that America’s markets remain the most innovative, liquid, and well-regulated in the world. Instead of being forced to turn to offshore, unregulated venues to access equity perpetual futures, Americans may now access equity perps on CFTC-regulated markets subject to robust safeguards. I appreciate the continued partnership of @SECGov and @SECPaulSAtkins as we work to further harmonize our agencies' regulatory initiatives.

The agency’s goal is to bring back into the U.S. legal field billions in volume that had been flowing to offshore crypto platforms. The instrument is being launched under the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000 (CFMA), which eliminates the need to pass new laws.

The regulator’s pragmatic step directly boosts Hyperliquid’s capitalization. Through its HIP-3 framework (in particular, the trade[XYZ] platform), the project already controls the largest on-chain market for perps on Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, with daily turnover in the hundreds of millions of dollars.

The new CFTC classification fully matched the structure that the Hyperliquid Policy Center advocated in official submissions to the authorities.

Now financial giant ICE (owner of the NYSE), which previously invested in trade[XYZ], gets a legal basis for creating a regulated American platform on Hyperliquid technology, while Payward (Kraken’s parent company) is accelerating the launch of a similar product through the regulated exchange Bitnomial.

Despite legalization in the U.S., Hyperliquid maintains a strict geoblock for American residents, continuing to serve the global market thanks to its key trump cards: on-chain liquidity, 24/7 trading and flexible margin conditions.

Local exchanges in the U.S. will inevitably face the limitations of traditional Wall Street sessions and strict SEC leverage limits in the early stages.

This moves Hyperliquid from the status of an offshore experiment into the role of the main technology donor of the American financial market, with the possibility of monetizing its infrastructure through fee opportunities from the trades of regulated partners.

The market instantly priced these prospects into the asset’s value. TradingView charts recorded a vertical surge in the HYPE/USD pair immediately after the release was published at 14:02 UTC: the price impulsively broke out of the $84.9-$85.30 corridor tested a local high above $87.40 and consolidated around $86.83, holding a net gain of more than 2%.

#5412. 99% Cold Wallet Rule Mulled by South Korea Following Binance Hack

South Korean financial regulators are reportedly considering introducing much stricter cryptocurrency storage requirements for local exchanges following the massive $6.3 billion Binance hack.

According to a Nov. 3 report by South Korean news outlet News1, the country’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) is discussing raising the minimum proportion of customer cryptocurrencies that exchanges must store in cold wallets from the current 80% to approximately 99%.

The potential regulatory change comes just days after Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, suffered one of the biggest security breaches in cryptocurrency history.

However, the proposed 99% threshold remains under discussion, and no official decision has been made.

Under South Korea’s existing Virtual Asset User Protection Act, cryptocurrency exchanges are required to store at least 80% of customers’ digital assets in cold wallets.

Unlike hot wallets, which are connected to the internet and used to process everyday transactions, cold wallets are kept offline, making them significantly less vulnerable to remote hacking attacks.

However, the proportion of assets stored offline varies significantly among South Korea’s leading cryptocurrency exchanges.

According to Financial Supervisory Service data cited by local media, Upbit currently has one of the highest cold wallet storage ratios in the country.

As of the end of September, the exchange held approximately 99.17% of customer assets in cold wallets.

Meanwhile, rival cryptocurrency exchange Bithumb stored approximately 94.76% of its assets offline, while Coinone’s cold wallet ratio stood at 85%.

#5411. China’s Largest Startup Deal Ever Lifts Global Venture Funding To $59B In October

Global venture funding in October totaled $59 billion, a 45% jump from a year earlier, per Crunchbase data, in large part due to a record-setting deal for China’s DeepSeek. The company’s $15.9 billion funding round marked the largest-ever venture deal for a Chinese company ever, and came in the same month that two other frontier labs raised blockbuster Series A rounds totaling at or close to $1 billion.

The bulk of October’s venture funding was invested in the two leading countries for startup investment, with companies based in the U.S. and China raising $28 billion and $20.6 billion last month, respectively. The last time more than $20 billion was invested in China in a single month was June 2018, when Ant Group raised $14 billion in its Series C funding.

Funding concentrated in seven companies that raised billion-dollar rounds, accounting for just over 40% of October’s venture funding. These large amounts were invested in frontier labs, manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, prediction markets and spend management software. Private equity led much of this funding, along with a few multistage venture firms including Sequoia Capital, Index Ventures and Lux Capital.

DeepSeek’s $15.9 billion raise at a valuation of $90 billion marked the largest private funding by a Chinese tech company on record. The deal places DeepSeek among the Top 10 most highly funded private companies. It also makes it the second most highly valued Chinese company after ByteDance, and the third most highly valued private frontier lab after U.S. companies Anthropic and OpenAI.

DeepSeek wasn’t the only Chinese frontier lab to raise big in October. Moonshot AI, a rival open-source lab, reportedly reached a $50 billion value in October, making it the 11th most valuable private company on The Crunchbase Unicorn Board. The startup has also reportedly confidentially filed to go public on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Massachusetts-based manufacturing startup Re:Build raised the second-largest funding deal last month, a $2.1 billion round. The company partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production and says it has 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity.

Other large rounds last month went to Axiom, which raised $2 billion for power and grid capacity build out for data centers; spend-management platform Ramp, which raised $1.85 billion and said its ARR has reached $2 billion; open-source semiconductor company Tenstorrent, which says it  raised a $1.5 billion Series E funding and recently moved its  headquarters to Silicon Valley from Canada; prediction market Kalshi, which raised a $1 billion Series E; and frontier lab Flapping Airplanes, which raised a $1 billion Series A.

A further eight companies raised rounds north of $500 million last month. They spanned industries ranging from frontier labs, robotics, legal and chips, to agentic AI and healthcare. Among the most notable was TypeSafe AI, which says it raised an $870 million Series A funding on the heels of rapid developer adoption of its decision model Jev.

A total of 66% of global funding was in AI-driven companies in October, with semiconductor companies gaining market share this past month.

The U.S. IPO market was slow in anticipation of Anthropic’s November IPO. The offering could surpass even SpaceX’s record-setting June listing that raised $85.7 billion.

On the M&A front, at least nine venture-backed companies were acquired for more than $1 billion last month, including Uber’s acquisition of 19-year-old ezCater for $2.3 billion.

With two months remaining, 2026 has already set records for acquisitions, IPOs and funding rounds across major venture markets. October extended that momentum, but also highlighted how concentrated this cycle has become: Seven companies accounted for more than 40% of global funding, while AI-driven businesses captured two-thirds.

The question heading into year-end is how widely that momentum will spread, as Anthropic prepares to list in what could be the largest IPO of all time.

The data contained in this report comes directly from Crunchbase, and is based on reported data. Data is as of Nov. 2, 2026.

#5410. Crypto Stocks Edge Up Before the Bell as 50 Companies Now Block Tokenized Shares: What Is Happening in the Market?

Crypto stocks edged higher before Tuesday’s open, November 3, even as Nvidia, Costco and Nike joined the companies blocking tokenized versions of their shares on OKXICE, taking the count to 50, and an AI chip sell-off sent Seoul’s Kospi down 3.6%.

The bounce is small, and it follows a bad month. Coinbase traded at $138.74 at 13:00 UTC, up 0.7% from Monday’s close of $137.83, its lowest finish since February 2024. Robinhood, Strategy and Circle rose between 0.5% and 1.1%, and Galaxy led with 2.8% after losing 8.8% on Monday.

The bigger story for the sector is the pushback against tokenization. Objectors to OKXICE, the 24/7 venue for tokenized US stocks that OKX is building with NYSE owner ICE, went from 16 to 50 in 11 days. Today is the deadline for companies notified on October 4, so the list could still grow, while Coinbase, Robinhood and the other crypto names on it have yet to say no.

Asia offered no lift. After a 1.1% drop in the Nasdaq on Monday, Samsung and SK hynix dragged the Kospi to 5,648.79, Shanghai slipped 0.8%, and Tokyo was shut for a holiday. Only Hong Kong closed higher, and Bitcoin held steady through the session at $77,326.

Investors are DUMPING US tech stocks at a rapid pace:The Nasdaq 100 index has dropped -6.1% over the last 3 trading sessions, its biggest 3-day decline since the April 2025 Liberation Day selloff. $QQQ This also marks the 3rd-largest 3-day decline since the 2022 bear market.… pic.twitter.com/jNvmex3HZj

So why are so many companies saying no to tokenization, and why are markets red from Seoul to New York?

Because they would carry the risk and see little of the benefit. OKXICE, the venue OKX is building with NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange, wants to offer round-the-clock trading of US stocks as tokens, paid for in stablecoins.

Under the SEC’s exemption, a company can keep its shares off such a venue if an outside firm does the tokenizing. It has 30 days from notice to object, and the objections have come fast:

The newest 12 are Nvidia, Costco, Micron, CrowdStrike, Corning, IREN, USA Rare Earth, Bloom Energy, Nike, Palo Alto Networks, Reddit and Hewlett Packard Enterprise. They join Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan, which runs its own blockchain unit and says it still likes the technology.

The fight is over shareholder rights, especially votes. “Right now companies like Goldman and Microsoft see all of the risk and none of the upside,” Injective’s COO Mirza Uddin told CNBC.

OKXICE co-chair Andrew Cuomo isn’t backing down. “We are at the very beginning of the rollout of fundamentally different market structure,” he said at the October 30 press conference.

Discover: JPMorgan and Coca-Cola Block Tokenized Stocks on OKXICE as Objectors Hit 33. Coinbase and Robinhood Stay Out of the List

Only the crypto names avoided objection to tokenisation, along with several major US stocks. Coinbase, Robinhood, Circle, Strategy, BitGo and Securitize remain outside the objection list, as do Apple, Amazon, Tesla, SpaceX and Netflix.

One crypto-born company did say no. IREN, the Bitcoin miner that now earns more from renting computers to AI firms than from mining, objected in the latest batch.

Silence isn’t a yes, though. Venues get up to five business days to publish objections, so companies that answered this week may not show up until next week’s notice, and staying off the list doesn’t guarantee a stock will trade at launch.

The AI trade is cracking again. Big Tech results last week showed Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft will keep spending heavily on data centres and chips, and investors want to see faster returns first.

Monday’s selling on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq fell 1.1%, hit Asia’s chipmakers on Tuesday:

Seoul’s slide is the one to watch. The Kospi closed at a record 9,114.55 on June 22 and is now 38% lower, with 17% of that lost since the end of September.

Oil added to the strain. Brent climbed 1.7% to $106.58 after reports of limited US strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after it fell more than 7% on hopes of new talks.

Hong Kong’s crypto stocks split. Exchange operator OSL rose 0.4%, and Boyaa Interactive, which holds Bitcoin, fell 5.1%.

They have been sold off with tech, then sold again for crypto. Every big name is down at least 12% since the end of September, and the first trading day after the Binance hack was the worst of the run.

Coinbase’s daily chart shows how far the slide has gone. The stock is $34 under its 50-day average and more than $50 under its 200-day, and Monday’s close was the lowest since February 2024.

COIN 1D chart. Source: Yahoo Finance (Nasdaq).

The tokenization fight won’t move share prices on its own. For crypto stocks, today’s pre-market bounce still has to survive Wall Street’s open and a long night of election results.

#5409. Ex-XRP Treasury Reveals Exit From $5 Million Stake in Ripple

A fresh annual report of British company VivoPower PLC, filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 2, 2026, officially disclosed the parameters of the closure of its cryptocurrency strategy.

The documents recorded the creation and subsequent liquidation of a $5 million stake in the private company Ripple Labs, while also making public the price of their buyback at $300 apiece.

According to the filing, in May 2025, VivoPower announced a large-scale treasury expansion with a target investment volume of up to $100 million in XRP tokens and Ripple Labs equity. In practice, the investments turned out to be more modest: the XRP treasury allocated $5.0 million to the direct acquisition of 41,810 Ripple Labs shares in January 2026.

For institutional investors, buying stakes in the fintech giant itself was a key way to make a large bet on the ecosystem's success.

However, the experiment lasted only nine months from its announcement. As early as February, VivoPower's board of directors decided to fully wind down the crypto direction. Management recognized holding digital assets as less profitable than developing artificial intelligence infrastructure and redirected capital to the purchase of a 41.5 MW data center in Mo i Rana, Norway, for $37.7 million.

The process of liquidating this $5 million stake brought the crypto market an important price insight. In April 2026, Ripple Labs conducted a targeted buyback, taking 882 shares from VivoPower at $300 apiece. The deal brought the British company $264,600 in cash and $159,122 in net profit, giving the community a rare and hard marker of how Ripple's management itself values its business in private trades.

A direct sale of the remaining part of the stake on the open market proved impossible due to the non-public status of the securities. As a result, VivoPower entered into agreements to sell the economic rights to the shares to two South Korean partners, KWeather Co. and Lean Ventures.

As of the filing date, the Korean deals have not yet been legally completed. The remaining 40,928 shares are locked in the Korea Securities Depository (KSD) under a strict one-year lock-up restriction. Due to this freeze and the lack of market liquidity, independent appraisers lowered the book value of this stake to $4.3 million (about $106.16 per share).

The VivoPower story clearly showed the crypto industry the flip side of institutional investments: a direct purchase of stakes in Ripple Labs comes with strict lock-ups and low liquidity, where the only fast source of fiat for exiting the ecosystem is the issuer itself through a private buyback procedure.

#5408. Most Venture Capital Is Going To Companies That Are Founded Or Led By Billionaires

The majority of U.S. venture capital nowadays goes to companies founded or led by men who are already billionaires.

This is not a difficult stat to unearth. So far this year, just seven companies raised more than half of all seed- through growth-stage investment. They’re mostly familiar names: OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI (now part of SpaceX), Anduril Industries, Databricks, Prometheus and The Boring Co.

These companies raised more than $260 billion in equity funding in the first 10 months of the year. That’s just over 50% of the U.S. seed and venture investment over the same period, per Crunchbase data.

Founders and CEOs of these seven companies are also well-known — and exceptionally  well-off to boot.

Two founders are particularly famous. They are the world’s wealthiest men: Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos.

Musk founded xAI and The Boring Co., and also co-founded OpenAI, (though he has no known equity stake in the latter). And while outside investors funded these companies, Musk could have also afforded to do so himself.

Ditto for Bezos, who in 2025 launched the physical AI startup Prometheus, which raised $12 billion earlier this year. Bezos’ own net worth, meanwhile, is calculated at more than $350 billion.

The two highest valuation startups — OpenAI and the soon-to-be-public Anthropic — also have prominent billionaire founders and CEOs. However, they have mixed backstories to their wealth.

OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman primarily made his vast wealth through investments in Y Combinator startups, including Stripe and Reddit. Altman has said he does not have an equity stake in OpenAI beyond a sliver from an old YC round. Co-founder Greg Brockman, by contrast, has a larger stake in OpenAI that was reportedly valued around $30 billion earlier this year.

At Anthropic, meanwhile, all seven company co-founders have similar-sized equity stakes, and each is worth billions. This includes the AI giant’s most famous co-founder, CEO Dario Amodei.

Databricks and Anduril, meanwhile, both have founders serving as CEOs who have amassed billion-dollar-plus net worths during their tenures.

Databricks co-founder and CEO Ali Ghodsi has a reported $7.6 billion net worth, with the company he leads valued at around $190 billion following an August financing.

Anduril co-founder and CEO Brian Schimpf, meanwhile, has an estimated $1.5 billion net worth as a result of his stake in the $61 billion valuation defense industry disruptor. Co-founder Palmer Luckey, who sold his virtual reality startup Oculus to Meta for $2 billion in 2014 before starting Anduril, has an estimated $5.9 billion net worth.

Several other founders and CEOs of startups that raised some of this year’s largest rounds are billionaires too. This includes Wonder founder Marc Lore, Figure founder Brett Adcock, and Surge AI founder and CEO Edwin Chen, among others.

We can split the billionaires who founded this year’s most heavily funded startups into two broad subcategories. There are those who became billionaires through the startup that just raised capital. And there are those who were already billionaires through prior companies or investments.

Ghodsi, Amodei and Brockman fit in the first group. In the second group, of course, we can put Musk and Bezos, as well as Altman and Luckey, who became a 21-year-old billionaire following the Oculus sale.

Historically, neither billionaire type was a particularly common recipient of venture funding rounds. The term “unicorn” as a moniker for private companies valued at $1 billion or more only entered the lexicon in 2013, when this asset class became noticeably large. In prior decades, founders and CEOs mostly only hit billionaire status after their startups went public or sold in high-priced acquisitions.

But times change. And in tandem, our image of what a startup funding recipient looks like should evolve as well.

True, quite a bit of capital still flows to the stereotypical venture recipients: first-time founders or serial entrepreneurs whose prior companies didn’t make them fabulously wealthy. But a majority of venture funding now does not go to these classic startup types.

Instead, it goes to companies with valuations already high enough to warrant billionaire status for their stakeholders as well as ventures founded by men who are already billionaires.

#5407. Tesla, Amazon Deal Fresh Blow to OKX Tokenization Push

OKX has suffered another big blow to its grand aspirations of tokenizing stocks after Tesla, Amazon, and four other big names turned down plans for the tokenization of their shares on the cryptocurrency exchange’s joint venture with New York Stock Exchange owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE).

Six new companies have raised objections to their shares being tokenized on the OKXICE platform.

Among the new objectors are Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX, e-commerce giant Amazon, streaming giant Netflix, semiconductor equipment maker Lam Research and fintech firm SoFi Technologies.

The new objections bring the total number of companies that have objected to the initiative to 56, further damaging OKX’s push into the realm of traditional finance.

In particular, five of the Magnificent Seven tech companies have turned down the proposal to have their stocks tokenized on the OKXICE platform. These include Tesla, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Nvidia.

What makes this rejection even more noteworthy is that the total number of targeted companies involved in this OKXICE joint venture is relatively low.

Back in early October, OKX and ICE announced their plan to offer tokenized versions of 62 major companies’ stocks.

However, 49 out of those 62 companies have formally opposed the proposal. Hence, about 79% of the initially targeted companies have rejected the plan. The other seven objections came from companies not in the initial selection.

Some of the most famous names in American finance and tech, including JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Walmart, Coca-Cola, Intel, Oracle, AMD, Nike and Costco, have also expressed their objections.

As of the Nov. 2 notice, only 13 out of the original selection had yet to raise a publicly disclosed objection.

These names include Apple, Coinbase, Robinhood, Strategy, Circle and Palantir.

However, the fact that they have not raised a formal objection doesn’t necessarily mean they approve of the tokenization plan.

It is worth noting that Nov. 3 marks the end of the 30-day objection period for the companies that received their initial notice on Oct. 4.

Nonetheless, with almost four-fifths of the initially targeted companies raising objections, OKXICE faces an uphill battle to get sufficient corporate involvement to make its tokenized stock market appealing to investors.

OKXICE has not set a definite launch date yet. It also has not disclosed the number of tokenized stocks it will offer when it starts trading.

#5406. XRP Price Prediction: Wall Street’s $28 Target Hinges on Supply Shock

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP is trading near $1.30 as institutional demand and tightening supply return to the spotlight. Standard Chartered still sees XRP price reaching $28 despite cutting its near-term prediction.

The bank’s target would require XRP to climb more than 2,000% from current levels. That makes institutional adoption and sustained buying pressure central to the bullish case.

U.S. spot XRP ETFs have accumulated 1.2 billion XRP since launching. Meanwhile, Ripple’s escrow system continues releasing tokens, creating a potential clash between institutional demand and available supply.

Standard Chartered’s Geoffrey Kendrick lowered his 2026 XRP price target to $2.80 earlier this year. However, the bank maintained its long-term forecast of $28 by 2030. Its revised roadmap projects XRP reaching $7 in 2027, $12.60 in 2028, and $19.60 in 2029. The final $28 target would represent an extraordinary recovery from current prices.

At approximately $1.30, XRP would need to gain around 2,050% to reach $28. Its market capitalization would approach $1.8 trillion using today’s circulating supply.

This valuation would place XRP among the world’s largest financial assets. ETF demand alone cannot justify such a move without substantial growth in adoption and liquidity.

Kendrick’s bullish thesis relies on institutional participation, regulatory clarity, and greater use of blockchain payment infrastructure. Spot ETFs provide one potential route for traditional investors to gain exposure.

The question now is whether those products can absorb enough XRP to influence market supply.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

U.S. spot XRP ETFs held 1.2 billion XRP by November 4. That accounts for 1.2% of the token’s fixed 100 billion maximum supply.

The funds have accumulated substantial holdings since their launch. However, recent flows show that institutional demand has not been consistently positive.

ETF data recorded outflows during several recent sessions, while October’s strongest buying days were followed by withdrawals. This could create a supply squeeze with renewed and sustained inflows.

If ETF demand accelerates, issuers must acquire XRP to support their products. Those purchases could reduce the amount of XRP readily available for trading, particularly if existing holders refuse to sell.

That dynamic could amplify price movements during periods of rising demand. A genuine supply shock would require persistent buying to overwhelm available sellers across exchanges and other markets.

Ripple’s escrow system adds another layer to the XRP price prediction. The company releases up to one billion XRP from escrow each month, with unused tokens often returned to new escrow contracts. Ripple is reportedly holding 31.7 billion XRP in escrow. Its total XRP holdings stood at 36.8 billion.

The negative impact of the 31 October release by Ripple of 300 million XRP from escrow🤣. $1.23 to $1.31. It’s as if XRP moves with the market or something. pic.twitter.com/OX3md8GTP1

But could XRP touch $28? The bullish scenario would require ETF purchases and institutional accumulation to outpace selling pressure. Greater use of XRP in payments and tokenized financial markets could provide additional demand.

XRP price remains far below Standard Chartered’s long-term prediction, for now. The token’s ability to hold recent support and attract renewed ETF inflows will help determine the supply-squeeze thesis and whether it can gain traction.

A sustained institutional buying cycle could strengthen the case for a much larger rally. Reaching $28, however, would require years of adoption growth beyond the ETF market alone.

#5405. Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse Breaks Silence on XRP vs. RLUSD Debate

Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse addressed the ongoing debate over the potential impact of Ripple’s RLUSD stablecoin on XRP’s future, asserting that both assets are complementary rather than competitive.

On Nov. 3, Brad Garlinghouse offered his view in response to a comprehensive X post from a notable member of the XRP Ledger community named Vet, who outlined the key differences between the two assets associated with Ripple.

“Well said, Vet. Complementary, not competitive,” the Ripple chief executive tweeted.

The brief statement comes amid pushback as some XRP holders are increasingly concerned that Ripple’s aggressive foray into the stablecoin market may negatively impact demand for XRP in the future.

As part of his viral post, Vet explained that the key difference between the two assets revolves around the purposes they serve on the XRP Ledger.

“RLUSD is optional. XRP isn’t,” the commentator explained.

As the XRP Ledger’s native currency, XRP is essential for the core functions of the network. First, every account must have an XRP reserve. Second, transaction fees are paid in XRP.

RLUSD, on the other hand, is a dollar-denominated stablecoin issued by Ripple's regulated stablecoin business. The key difference is that, unlike XRP, the value of RLUSD is supposed to remain stable at roughly $1.

Another key difference lies in control over the assets.

Ripple has the ability to freeze RLUSD under certain conditions, for example, to meet legal obligations. There is no central entity that can freeze XRP, the native cryptocurrency, on the ledger.

According to Vet, another key advantage of XRP is its privileged status on the XRP Ledger's DEX.

The XRP Ledger has an automatic bridging function. In this way, if it makes sense to trade between currencies through XRP for a better exchange rate, trades can be automatically routed through XRP.

This is why XRP is so valuable for liquidity providers and market makers as an intermediary asset.

On the other hand, RLUSD would be much more suitable in cases where price stability is important, for example, for payroll, invoicing, corporate payments, etc.

At the same time, some XRP investors are worried that one day RLUSD may effectively replace XRP for some payment use cases.

The crucial question is this: If you can send a dollar-denominated stablecoin directly, why would you need to use an intermediary like XRP?

It’s also worth noting that RLUSD isn’t exclusive to the XRP Ledger. In fact, RLUSD also works on Ethereum and other supported blockchains. So increasing demand for RLUSD doesn’t necessarily lead to more use of the XRP Ledger.

And even if we’re seeing more RLUSD transactions on the XRP Ledger, this doesn’t automatically mean that increased demand for XRP to pay transaction fees necessarily guarantees a significant price surge for the cryptocurrency.

It’s not the first time Garlinghouse has been forced to comment on Ripple's changing priorities.

During Ripple’s Swell 2026 conference in New York on Oct. 28, Ripple’s CEO directly addressed rumors that Ripple is becoming increasingly focused on RLUSD rather than XRP.

“We will never give up on XRP,” Garlinghouse said.

#5403. The Crunchbase Tech Layoffs Tracker

The past week has seen at least a dozen companies from both overseas and the U.S. reporting tech layoffs.

Leading by the count of workers affected is New South Wales, Australia-based Canva, an online design and visual communications platform. According to an update posted on its website, the company is reducing its global workforce by 22%, or 1,271 people. With workers based in Austin and San Francisco, it is unclear how many of those layoffs will affect U.S. employees.

Amazon rejoins the tracker this week with a pair of reported layoffs. The first involves 250 workers in its devices and services division, a cutback that took place last week, and another 95 employees in positions including software engineers, product managers and operations employees. According to a report in TheStreet, the affected workers are scheduled to be laid off between Dec. 7 and Jan. 25.

According to a report in the Sacramento Business Journal, Santa Clara, California-based Intel has laid off 67 workers from its Folsom, California, location.

In the lone shutdown reported this week, Ollie AI, a subscription-based AI assistant, will officially close the app on Nov. 6. According to a report in TechCrunch, Bill Lennon, the San Diego-based company’s co-founder and CEO, cited the pressures of the burgeoning AI industry, saying “We got close, but ultimately couldn’t keep up.”

The following companies were added to the tracker this week:

Layoffs during the weeks ended Nov. 4, 2026: At least 2,982 U.S. tech sector employees were laid off or scheduled for layoffs, per a Crunchbase News tally.

In 2025: Around 127,000 workers were let go from U.S.-based tech companies according to our tally.

In 2024: At least 95,667 workers at U.S.-based tech companies lost their jobs in 2024, according to a Crunchbase News tally.

In 2023: More than 191,000 workers in U.S.-based tech companies (or tech companies with a large U.S. workforce) were laid off in mass job cuts.

In 2022: More than 93,000 jobs were slashed from public and private tech companies in the U.S.

This tracker includes layoffs conducted by U.S.-based companies or those with a strong U.S. presence and is updated at least bi-weekly. We’ve included both startups and publicly traded, tech-heavy companies. We’ve also included companies based elsewhere that have a sizable team in the United States, such as Klarna, even when it’s unclear how much of the U.S. workforce has been affected by layoffs.

Layoff and workforce figures are best estimates based on reporting. We source the layoffs from media reports, our own reporting, social media posts and layoffs.fyi, a crowdsourced database of tech layoffs.

We recently updated our layoffs tracker to reflect the most recent round of layoffs each company has conducted. This allows us to quickly and more accurately track layoff trends, which is why you might notice some changes in our most recent numbers.

If an employee headcount cannot be confirmed to our standards, we note it as “unclear.”

A layoff can be either a permanent termination of someone’s employment — usually for cost-saving reasons — or a temporary one because there’s not enough work to justify a full workforce. Tech company layoffs generally fall into the permanent category.

A mass layoff is when a significant number of a company’s employees are cut in a short period of time, often as a result of economic conditions.

Tech layoffs started to surge in 2022 and continued in 2023 and 2024. Companies have given various reasons for conducting layoffs.

Some companies — especially those in the e-commerce sector — nearly doubled their employee headcount to meet consumer demand during the COVID-19 pandemic’s stay-at-home mandates, and later found that they were overstaffed as daily life returned to normal.

Large tech employers such as Salesforce and Google parent Alphabet noted that their post-pandemic layoffs followed several years of rapid hiring fueled by fast growth — between 2019 and 2022, some companies nearly doubled their employee headcount. Some large tech companies also cited slowing sales and fears of a recession as reasons for downsizing.

Venture-backed startups, meanwhile, also cut jobs as a way to cut costs and preserve their cash reserves, as venture funding fell significantly after the peak in 2021. Some startups that ran out of cash and couldn’t raise new funding found themselves filing for bankruptcy or shutting down.

Intel Corp. laid off the largest number of people among U.S. tech employers in 2024, by our count. The semiconductor giant laid off more than 15,000 employees last year.

It was followed closely by electric-car maker Tesla, which cut more than 14,000 roles, and networking company Cisco, with more than 10,000 total roles cut.

In 2023, Amazon layoffs led the numbers with 16,000 roles cut. Layoffs at Alphabet, the parent company of Google, totaled about 12,000, and Microsoft’s layoffs totaled about 10,000 workers in 2023, as did Facebook parent Meta’s layoffs.

Many venture-backed tech startups have also done layoffs as venture capital investment has fallen sharply since the peak in 2021, and falling startup valuations factor into their decisions to conduct layoffs.

Yes, more layoffs are likely coming. While there are signs that the volume of layoffs is tapering, experts we talked to expect job cuts in the tech sector to continue for the foreseeable future as large tech companies and startups continue to battle economic headwinds.

Seed and early-stage startups in particular may continue to conduct layoffs in an attempt to extend their cash runways in a difficult venture funding environment.

Tech layoffs noticeably increased at the start of 2022, ramped up in 2023, waned somewhat in 2024 and have continued in 2025.

Signs that may indicate a company is more likely to conduct layoffs include:

Layoffs declined in 2024 compared to the previous year, but are expected to continue into 2025, although likely not at the level seen in 2023. Startups that need to preserve cash to extend their runways are more likely to conduct layoffs.

Tech layoffs will likely slow when venture capital funding increases and the startup economy stabilizes, as well as when market conditions improve and more startups gain liquidity via IPOs.

Startups that raised capital during the venture funding heyday at inflated valuations in 2021 are more likely to need to conduct layoffs if they’re not able to sustain their previous valuations or growth projections.

Tech layoffs started surging in the 2022 market correction, with an estimated 93,000 U.S. tech workers laid off that year. That figure more than doubled in 2023, with around 200,000 U.S. tech employees laid off, according to our Tech Layoffs Tracker. Layoffs abated again in 2024, with around 95,000 reported tech layoffs.

Keep in mind, many companies don’t report detailed layoffs figures, and some companies continue hiring after cuts for positions deemed more beneficial to the business.

No, according to experts in the sector, who say a sale is unlikely to solve a tech company’s cash-flow issues.

This is especially true as fewer startup M&A deals are happening in the current downturn.

Tech layoffs have hit across departments at many companies.

Many layoffs from the large tech giants were software engineers. Startups tend to be more likely to retain engineers in favor of doing layoffs in their talent and recruiting, marketing and other departments.

Google cut roles in its sales, recruiting, product and engineering teams. Amazon layoffs included jobs in its AWS cloud unit, at its social video platform Twitch, and in its advertising department. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company’s recruiting department would be the first to see job cuts.

Follow all of our tech layoffs news here and track which companies are cutting jobs with the layoffs tracker above.

While not daily, this Crunchbase Tech Layoffs Tracker is updated weekly, if not more frequently, with the latest job cuts at U.S. tech employers.

Many tech companies continue to hire for open roles, despite layoffs in the sector. Find out more about Crunchbase’s Actively Hiring filter and how you can find companies with multiple open roles.

You can find all of our job market-related news here.

#5402. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5401. Binance Hacker Continues Aggressive Bitcoin Buying Spree

The hacker behind the monumental Binance attack is still buying up more Bitcoin (BTC).

As per the latest blockchain analytics data from Lookonchain dated Nov. 4, the hacker continues to exchange SOL for Bitcoin, moving the stolen assets across several crypto wallets.

The blockchain tracker added that the hacker is using the following multi-step process to exchange the stolen crypto for Bitcoin.

The hacker’s complicated scheme involves splitting his SOL assets among different wallets before selling the SOL for USDC, transferring the USDC from Solana to Ethereum, buying ETH using the USDC and finally exchanging the newly bought ETH for BTC using THORChain, a decentralized cross-chain liquidity protocol.

This long and complicated cross-chain transaction process allows the hacker to easily transfer his funds between different blockchain networks. It also makes it harder to trace the stolen assets.

This in not the first time that the hacker has been buying Bitcoin with the stolen funds. In fact, he had earlier been seen making transactions to buy Bitcoin using tens of millions of dollars’ worth of stolen SOL.

As per Lookonchain’s data dated Nov. 1, the hacker behind the Binance hack was trying to convert approximately 970,522 SOL, worth roughly $95.9 million at the time of writing, into Bitcoin.

The hacker was even seen making a transaction involving 486,970 SOL (approximately $46.4M) in just one hour.

However, during these transactions, the hacker used a different service called Relay Protocol, which also allows cross-chain crypto transfers.

From the recent blockchain data, it looks like the hacker is still focused on Bitcoin. He’s also using several decentralized services to exchange the stolen crypto.

The latest official update from Binance shows that the massive security breach has affected crypto assets worth around $6.34 billion.

As per the update, the exchange says that it has frozen/intercepted about $2.85 billion worth of stolen cryptocurrency as of Nov. 3.

According to US federal authorities, the attack was conducted by a North Korean state-sponsored hacker group called TraderTraitor.

The FBI is also asking various decentralized crypto services like THORChain to prevent funds linked to the attack from moving around.

Even with all these efforts, the latest on-chain data shows that the hacker is still moving stolen funds across different networks.
